title: Overfitting checks: holdout & walk-forward
subtitle: Who checks what, in plain words

sections.title: What overfitting is
beats: Overfitting = a model memorizes the past instead of learning a real pattern.
It looks great on old data and falls apart on new data.
The cure: always judge it on data it never saw while tuning.
sections.example: Memorizing last year's test answers vs actually learning the subject.
sections.sayback: Say why a perfect backtest is a warning sign.

quiz.a: Great on training data, bad on new data.

sections.title: Holdout & walk-forward
beats: Holdout: hide the last chunk of data (say 30%). Tune on the rest. Test once on the hidden part.
Walk-forward: tune on months 1–3, test on 4. Slide: tune 2–4, test 5. Repeat.
Walk-forward fits trading because markets change over time.
sections.example: A paper-trading phase is a forward test: trades settled on real prices the bot never tuned on.

quiz.q: Why test only once on the holdout?
quiz.a: Each extra peek leaks it into tuning, so it stops being unseen.

sections.tieback: Idea only: a script could replay closed trades and report scorecard per walk-forward window.

sections.title: The calibration haircut
beats: Calibration = when the model says 70%, does it win about 70%?
A haircut = stated confidence − real hit rate, kept inside safe bounds (e.g., 0 to 0.3).
Overconfident models get marked down automatically.
Small samples are noisy. 10 trades can't prove much, so the bounds and 1-step limits matter.
sections.example: Says 80%, wins 60% → haircut 0.2 → future 80% calls treated as 60%.
sections.sayback: Why clamp the haircut instead of letting it go anywhere?
